page: Amazon Web Services c8gb.metal-24xl is a bare-metal, compute-optimized instance built on the 64-bit ARM architecture. The host is powered by 96 dedicated physical cores running at a base clock frequency of 2.8 GHz, providing 96 total vCPUs without simultaneous multithreading. Memory capacity is provisioned at 192.0 GB, establishing a 1:2 core-to-memory ratio of 2.0 GB per physical core.

The system does not include integrated local disk storage, necessitating network-attached storage architectures for persistence. There are no discrete GPUs or accelerator modules present. To handle cluster interconnects and high-volume data transport, c8gb.metal-24xl provides a baseline network bandwidth of 200 Gbps. Complimentary public IPv4 addresses are not included.

Direct bare-metal access eliminates hypervisor overhead and resource contention, offering predictable single-thread and multi-core CPU execution. Given its high-density core configuration, dedicated execution pipelines, and substantial 200 Gbps networking, the instance is structured for distributed compute tasks, large-scale software compilation, continuous integration workflows, and network-intensive batch processing.
description: Amazon Web Services c8gb.metal-24xl is a bare-metal compute-optimized server based on 64-bit ARM architecture. Powered by dedicated AWS Graviton processors operating at 2.8 GHz, the system features 96 physical cores and 96 vCPUs with a single thread per core. It is configured with 192.0 GB of RAM, corresponding to an exact 2.0 GB per core allocation. The instance includes no integrated local storage or graphics processing units, relying entirely on remote storage. A major hardware feature is its baseline network throughput of 200 Gbps, which facilitates substantial inter-node communication. By removing virtualization overhead, c8gb.metal-24xl delivers full hardware-level isolation for compute-intensive workloads. The server fits high-performance batch processing, continuous integration, large-scale software compilation, distributed application microservices, and network-heavy compute jobs requiring consistent CPU utilization.
